title: Your MCP Tools Are Eating Your Context Window: Measure, Trim and Lazy-Load Tool Definitions in Python
author: EME GUG
summary:
Tuần trước mình debug một agent nội bộ: model chọn sai tool liên tục, response chậm, bill API tăng gần gấp đôi so với tháng trước. Code agent không đổi gì, prompt cũng không đổi. Hóa ra team vừa cắm thêm 3 MCP server (GitHub, Postgres, Jira), tổng cộng hơn 90 tool. Request nào cũng phải gửi kèm toàn bộ định nghĩa tool, trước khi user kịp gõ chữ nào đã mất khoảng 38.000 token . Bài này chia sẻ cách mình đo chi phí đó, cắt gọn schema và chuyển sang lazy-load tool, để agent vừa rẻ hơn vừa chọn tool chính xác hơn. Vì sao MCP tool lại tốn context đến vậy Khi agent kết nối tới một MCP server, client gọi tools/list và nhận về danh sách tool, mỗi tool gồm name , description và inputSchema (JSON Schema). Phần lớn framework đưa toàn bộ danh sách này vào mọi request gửi tới LLM. Hậu quả: Chi phí cố định cho mỗi request : 90 tool × ~400 token mỗi tool = 36k token, kể cả khi user chỉ hỏi chào buổi sáng. Model chọn tool kém đi : càng nhiều tool trùng ý nghĩa ( search_issues , search_code , search_jira ...) thì model càng dễ chọn nhầm. Còn ít chỗ cho dữ liệu thật : context dành cho file, log, kết quả query bị thu hẹp. flowchart LR U[User message] --> A[Agent] S1[GitHub MCP
35 tools] --> A S2[Postgres MCP
20 tools] --> A S3[Jira MCP
38 tools] --> A A -->|system + 93 tool schemas + message| L[LLM] L --> R[~38k token overhead mỗi request] Trước khi tối ưu thì phải đo đã. Đừng đoán. Bước 1: Đo số token của từng MCP server Mình dùng mcp Python SDK (bản 1.x) để kết nối tới server qua stdio, lấy danh sách tool rồi đếm token. Ở đây mình dùng tiktoken với encoding cl100k_base để ước lượng. Tokenizer của mỗi model sẽ lệch một chút, nhưng để so sánh tương đối giữa các server thì dùng được. python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install "mcp>=1.2" tiktoken # measure_tools.py import asyncio , json , sys import tiktoken from mcp import ClientSession , StdioServerParameters from mcp . client . stdio import stdio_client enc = tiktoken . get_encoding ( "cl100k_base" ) def tool_tokens ( tool ) -> int : payload = { "name" : tool . name , "description" : tool . description or "" , "input_schema" : tool . inputSchema , } return len ( enc . encode ( json . dumps ( payload , ensure_ascii = False ) ) ) async def measure ( command : str , args : list [ str ] ) : params = StdioServerParameters ( command = command , args = args ) async with stdio_client ( params ) as ( read , write ) : async with ClientSession ( read , write ) as session : await session . initialize ( ) result = await session . list_tools ( ) rows = sorted ( ( ( t . name , tool_tokens ( t ) ) for t in result . tools ) , key = lambda x : - x [ 1 ] , ) total = sum ( n for _ , n in rows ) print ( f "{len(rows)} tools, ~{total} tokens" ) for name , n in rows [ : 10 ] : print ( f " {n:>6} {name}" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : asyncio . run ( measure ( sys . argv [ 1 ] , sys . argv [ 2 : ] ) ) Chạy thử với filesystem server chính thức: python measure_tools.py npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /tmp Kết quả bên mình làm nhiều người bất ngờ: chỉ 10 tool chiếm tới 55% tổng token . Nguyên nhân thường là description dài như tài liệu hướng dẫn, có cả ví dụ, và schema có enum hàng chục giá trị hoặc object lồng 4-5 tầng. Bước 2: Cắt gọn schema trước khi đưa cho model Nhiều MCP server là của bên thứ ba nên mình không sửa trực tiếp được. Cách làm là thêm một lớp transform ở phía client: giữ nguyên tên tool để gọi lại server, chỉ rút gọn phần gửi cho LLM. # slim.py import copy DROP_KEYS = { "examples" , "$schema" , "additionalProperties" , "title" , "default" } MAX_DESC = 160 MAX_ENUM = 8 def slim_schema ( node ) : if isinstance ( node , dict ) : out = { } for k , v in node . items ( ) : if k in DROP_KEYS : continue if k == "description" and isinstance ( v , str ) : v = v . strip ( ) . split ( " " ) [ 0 ] [ : MAX_DESC ] if k == "enum" and isinstance ( v , list ) and len ( v ) > MAX_ENUM : # enum quá dài: bỏ enum, ghi gợi ý vào description out [ "description" ] = ( out . get ( "description" , "" ) + f " (một trong: {', '.join(map(str, v[:MAX_ENUM]))}, ...)" ) . strip ( ) continue out [ k ] = slim_schema ( v ) return out if isinstance ( node , list ) : return [ slim_schema ( x ) for x in node ] return node def slim_tool ( tool : dict ) -> dict : t = copy . deepcopy ( tool ) t [ "description" ] = ( t . get ( "description" ) or "" ) . split ( " " ) [ 0 ] [ : MAX_DESC * 2 ] t [ "input_schema" ] = slim_schema ( t [ "input_schema" ] ) return t Vài kinh nghiệm thực tế: Chỉ giữ đoạn đầu của description . Phần ví dụ dài thường không giúp model chọn đúng hơn. Không xóa required và type , nếu không model sẽ truyền sai argument và server trả lỗi validation. Phải test lại : sau khi slim, chạy bộ eval khoảng 50 prompt thật xem tỷ lệ chọn đúng tool có giảm không. Bên mình token giảm khoảng 40%, accuracy giữ nguyên. Bước 3: Lazy-load tool theo ngữ cảnh Slim schema chỉ giảm được tuyến tính. Muốn giảm mạnh hơn thì đừng gửi cả 93 tool nữa, mỗi lượt chỉ gửi top-k tool liên quan cộng với một meta-tool find_tools để model tự xin thêm khi cần. sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant R as Tool Router participant L as LLM participant M as MCP Servers U->>R: "Tạo issue cho bug login" R->>R: Rank 93 tools, chọn top 6 + find_tools R->>L: message + 7 tool schemas L->>R: call github.create_issue R->>M: tools/call M-->>R: result R-->>L: tool result L-->>U: Đã tạo issue #482 Router của mình viết rất đơn giản, chưa cần đến embedding. Chỉ dùng BM25 trên name + description , với ~100 tool chạy chưa tới 1ms: # router.py (pip install rank-bm25) import re from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi def tokenize ( s : str ) -> list [ str ] : return re . findall ( r "[a-z0-9]+" , s . lower ( ) . replace ( "_" , " " ) ) class ToolRouter : def __init__ ( self , tools : list [ dict ] , always_on : set [ str ] = frozenset ( ) ) : self . tools = tools self . always_on = always_on self . bm25 = BM25Okapi ( [ tokenize ( t [ "name" ] + " " + t [ "description" ] ) for t in tools ] ) def select ( self , query : str , k : int = 6 ) -> list [ dict ] : scores = self . bm25 . get_scores ( tokenize ( query ) ) ranked = sorted ( zip ( scores , self . tools ) , key = lambda x : - x [ 0 ] ) picked = [ t for s , t in ranked [ : k ] if s > 0 ] picked += [ t for t in self . tools if t [ "name" ] in self . always_on and t not in picked ] return picked + [ FIND_TOOLS ] FIND_TOOLS = { "name" : "find_tools" , "description" : "Tìm thêm tool nếu các tool hiện có không phù hợp. Trả về tên + mô tả ngắn." , "input_schema" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "query" : { "type" : "string" } } , "required" : [ "query" ] } , } Khi model gọi find_tools , router chạy select(query, k=5) và thêm các tool đó vào danh sách cho lượt kế tiếp, các tool đã chọn từ trước vẫn giữ lại. Lưu ý quan trọng: giữ thứ tự tool ổn định giữa các lượt. Nếu provider của bạn có prompt caching, xáo trộn danh sách tool sẽ làm cache miss liên tục và mất luôn phần lợi vừa có được. Kết quả sau 2 tuần chạy production: token đầu vào trung bình giảm từ ~41k xuống ~9k mỗi request, tỷ lệ chọn sai tool giảm khoảng 1/3 (do ít tool "na ná nhau" hơn). Model gọi find_tools ở khoảng 7% số lượt, đổi lại tốn thêm một round-trip, chấp nhận được. Kết luận MCP giúp cắm tool vào agent dễ như cắm USB, nhưng chính vì dễ nên chúng ta hay cắm quá tay. Checklist mình áp dụng cho mọi agent: Đo trước : chạy measure_tools.py cho từng server, ghi lại số token vào README nội bộ hoặc CI. Server nào vượt 5k token thì phải review. Chỉ bật tool thực sự dùng : nhiều client hỗ trợ allowlist tool. Một GitHub server 35 tool mà bạn chỉ dùng 6 thì tắt 29 tool kia đi. Slim schema ở phía client : cắt description, bỏ examples và enum dài. Nhớ chạy eval trước và sau khi slim. Lazy-load khi có trên ~30 tool : BM25 router + meta-tool find_tools là đủ để bắt đầu, chưa cần vector DB. Giữ thứ tự tool ổn định để không phá prompt cache. Theo dõi liên tục : log input_tokens theo từng request. Khi ai đó cắm thêm MCP server mới, bạn sẽ thấy ngay trên dashboard thay vì đợi đến cuối tháng nhìn hóa đơn. Context window không phải tài nguyên miễn phí. Mỗi token dành cho định nghĩa tool không dùng tới là một token bớt đi cho dữ liệu thật mà agent cần để làm việc.

title: How much of your pool does the robot actually clean? A coverage simulator in 60 lines of Python
author: Adeline
summary: A distributor forwarded me a customer email last month. Two lines: "The robot runs for 40 minutes and the floor still looks striped. Is it broken?" stonebotclean.com The honest answer is that I didn't know. Every spec sheet in this category quotes a runtime, a swath width and a suction power. None of them quote coverage, because coverage is not a spec you can print — it is what happens when a path meets a rectangle with walls on four sides. So I stopped reading brochures and wrote a simulator. Rasterise the pool at 2 cm, stamp the brush along the path, count how many cells never get touched. Here is what came out, and the three things I got wrong on the first pass. ** The model Nothing fancy. A 12 × 6 m pool (72 m², a normal residential rectangle), a 42 cm effective swath, 0.28 m/s while scrubbing, 6 s for a 180° lane change, 15 cm of standoff so the brush housing clears the wall, and a 150 minute battery. Four serpentine variants, differing only in lane pitch: pitch = 1.00 × swath (0.42 m): the textbook answer, lanes exactly tangent pitch = 0.85 × swath (0.36 m): 15% overlap pitch = 0.70 × swath (0.29 m): 30% overlap pitch = 1.30 × swath (0.55 m): what happens when someone tunes the lane spacing up to "finish faster" Plus one control: a random-bounce run with no planning at all — drive until you hit a wall, deflect, keep going, change heading roughly every 8 seconds. That is what a $300 hobby unit does, and it is the baseline every lidar-equipped robot is implicitly being compared against. The measurement is a disk stamp: at every 4 cm along the path, mark every 2 cm cell within 10.5 cm of the centre as cleaned. Then count. def boustrophedon(pitch, pool, bot): L, W = pool["length"], pool["width"] stand, w = bot["standoff"], bot["width"] x0, x1 = stand, L - stand y0, y1 = stand, W - stand lane_y, y = [], y0 + w / 2 while y <= y1 - w / 2 + 1e-9: lane_y.append(y) y += pitch if lane_y[-1] < y1 - w / 2 - 1e-6: # edge pass lane_y.append(y1 - w / 2) ... That edge pass line is the first thing I got wrong. Without it, the loop stops as soon as the next lane would cross the top wall, and the last 28 cm of the pool simply never gets driven. On the 15% overlap run that was 4.9% of the floor — invisible in a spec sheet, visible to anyone standing at the shallow end. What the numbers said Strategy Lane pitch Floor reached Time Swept area / floor Lane changes Tangent lanes 0.42 m 99.66% 11.9 min 1.03× 13 15% overlap 0.36 m 100.00% 13.4 min 1.17× 15 30% overlap 0.29 m 100.00% 15.8 min 1.37× 18 Over-spaced 0.55 m 80.69% 9.5 min 0.83× 10 Random bounce, 1 charge — 100.00% 150 min 13.68× 1,507 Random bounce, 3 charges — 100.00% 450 min 41.20× 4,277 ** Finding one: tangent lanes lose 0.34% of the floor to pinholes. 99.66% sounds like rounding. It isn't. When lane centres sit exactly one swath apart, the brushes are tangent, and any raster cell on the boundary line between two lanes has a fighting chance of being missed. In the picture that shows up as a hairline of uncleaned floor every 42 cm — the "striped" look, at one-pixel width. In a real pool, a 1 cm strip is not a defect you can see. In a real pool with 3° of yaw drift and a slightly conical brush, it is. Finding two: 15% overlap costs 1.5 minutes and buys the last 0.34%. 200.7 m of path instead of 177.3 m, 15 lane changes instead of 13, 13.4 minutes instead of 11.9. Sweep ratio goes from 1.03× to 1.17× — 17% more brush passes over the same floor. That is a cheap insurance policy against yaw drift, brush wear and a slightly out-of-square pool. 30% overlap buys nothing the 15% run didn't already have, and costs 2.4 more minutes plus 17% more brush passes over the floor. If you have to pick one number for a lane pitch, it is around 0.85 × swath, not 1.0. Finding three: over-spaced lanes are the only strategy that fails visibly, and it fails fast. 0.55 m pitch finishes in 9.5 minutes — the fastest run in the table, 29% quicker than the 15% overlap case. It also misses 19.3% of the reachable floor in 19 cm stripes. This is the exact trade a manufacturer makes when the marketing number is "cleans your pool in 10 minutes", and it is why customers write emails about stripes. Fast, and visibly wrong. Finding four: random bounce reaches 100%, which is the least useful 100% in the table. The unplanned run covers every cell inside one 150-minute charge. It also sweeps 13.7 times the floor area to do it — 2,344 m driven, 1,507 wall nudges — which is 11× the runtime of a planned 13.4 minute run. So "coverage" alone cannot rank these strategies. Two numbers, not one: how much of the floor, and how much work per square metre. A lidar robot that plans lanes is not selling coverage. Coverage was never the hard part. It is selling the 1.17×. Bonus, because it surprised me: turning is 11% of the runtime. At 6 s per lane change, the 15% overlap run spends 90 of its 804 seconds rotating. On a 6 m width that is fine. Halve the pool width and the lane count barely changes; double it and you are spending a fifth of your battery on pirouettes. Lane pitch affects runtime twice — once through path length, once through lane count. Where the model lies I would rather list this than have someone in the comments list it for me. The drive is lossless. No slip, no wheel scrub on the tiles, no slowdown in the shallow end, no current. Real units lose 5–15% of nominal speed and lose most of it on turns. The swath is a perfect disk. Real suction mouths lose width at the edges and lose more when the filter is half-full. Effective width drops through a cycle. No dirt model. "Covered" means "the brush passed over it". Whether one pass removes algae film is a chemistry question I have no data for. Flat floor only. No slope, no steps, no main drain, no ladder. Wall climbing and waterline scrubbing are outside the raster entirely. The random run is friendly. 8 seconds between heading changes, no stalling in corners, no getting stuck on the drain cover. Real chaotic navigation is worse than this, so 13.7× is closer to a floor than a ceiling. One cycle, one direction. No multi-cycle accumulation, no slope-driven drift in the serpentine. Everything above is a constant at the top of the file. Change BOT["width"] to 0.28 and the whole table shifts; that is the point of writing it down instead of arguing about it. What I would add next Two things, in this order. First, yaw drift. Model the robot leaving each lane 2–3° off axis and let the error compound; that turns the pinhole problem from a raster artefact into a real stripe generator, and it will tell you whether 15% overlap is enough or whether you need 25%. Second, dirt-weighted coverage. Right now every square centimetre is worth the same. In reality the shallow end and the steps collect most of the debris, and a planner that spends its extra passes there is worth more than one that spends them evenly. That needs a weight map, which needs real pool data, which I do not have yet. Code, figures and the JSON output are all in one file, roughly 280 lines, numpy and matplotlib only: python pool_coverage_sim.py # writes results.json + figures/ If you build pool robots, the number I would like from you is not swath width. It is lane pitch, lane-change time, and whether the planner does an edge pass.

title: How our Pipeline orchestrates LBO Due Diligence ?
author: Thien Ban BUI
summary:
Welcome to the third chapter of our four-part series, **Building Sovereign, Hallucination-Free Financial AI . In Part 1: Building a Deterministic Financial Agent with Dual-Persona LoRA , we prohibited probabilistic language models from performing arithmetic. In Part 2: How our Training Recipe led us to "Hallucination" , we stepped into the machine room: fine-tuning an 8B model. Today, we address the ultimate frontier: What happens when the financial question cannot fit into a single prompt or table? How do we orchestrate complex, multi-step workflows like a Cross-Table LBO Due Diligence across disparate financial statements—and how do we ensure the final synthesis sent to the boardroom is 100% immune to semantic inversion and hallucination? 1. Why Fine-Tuning Alone Fails at Macro-Reasoning In Part 2 , we showed that when an 8B specialist model encounters missing variables in a messy financial filing, standard RLHF conditions it to panic: it grabs loosely related numbers from adjacent rows to satisfy the prompt, falling directly into the Compensation Hallucination Trap . We fixed this at the micro-level with response-only masking and rejection circuit breakers . But in enterprise finance, you quickly encounter a macro-level barrier: Imagine handing an autonomous agent an audited annual report (like the official French standalone filing — comptes sociaux — of Renault SAS , Renault Group's main operating subsidiary) and asking: "Is a leveraged buyout (LBO) of this target financially feasible based on its latest audited accounts?" Answering this is not a one-shot retrieval problem. It requires navigating across multiple disparate accounting schedules: Finding the operating subsidiary's Self-Financing Capacity ( CAPACITE D'AUTOFINANCEMENT , a proxy for pre-CapEx operating cash flow in French GAAP) in the Cash Flow Statement ( Tableau de Financement ). Cross-referencing current Financial Debt in Note E.4 of the balance sheet annex. Calculating the Debt-to-Cash Flow repayment horizon ( capacité de remboursement , a core French banking covenant using CAF as a pre-CapEx cash-flow proxy for EBITDA). Pulling Equity from Note E.1 to calculate balance sheet Gearing. Computing the operating margin buffer from the standalone Income Statement of Renault SAS ( RESULTAT D'EXPLOITATION / CHIFFRE D'AFFAIRES ). If you shove all these tables into a single context window and ask an 8B model to reason through all five steps at once, attention anxiety returns with a vengeance . The model conflates standalone operating subsidiary debt with consolidated group figures, divides equity by operating profit, or produces subtle, catastrophic semantic inversions. To solve this, we must enforce Separation of Concerns at the system architecture level. 2. The Generalist Crew Manager: Multi-Step DAG Orchestration Instead of burdening a single specialist model with planning, document navigation, tool invocation, and narrative synthesis, we architected a Bilateral Multi-Agent Hierarchy governed by Domain-Driven Design (DDD). What is a Multi-Step DAG? A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a deterministic task pipeline where execution flows strictly forward from prerequisites to dependent outputs ( Directed ) with zero infinite loops ( Acyclic ). Independent balance sheet extractions run in parallel, while cross-table ratios wait for their exact upstream inputs before converging into the final decision policy. flowchart TD User(["💼 Boardroom Prompt:
'Is an LBO takeover feasible?'"]) --> CrewMgr["👔 Generalist Crew Manager
(Hierarchical Task Planner & Arbiter)"] subgraph BilateralLoop ["🤝 Bilateral Multi-Agent Negotiation"] CrewMgr <-->|"1. Evaluates Balance Sheet Rubrics"| SpecAdv["🧠 Domain Specialist Advisor
(LboCovenantPolicyVO & Accounting Ontology)"] SpecAdv -->|"2. Proposes 5-Pillar Credit Plan"| DAG["⚡ Execution Plan (5-Step DAG)"] end subgraph ExecutionCore ["⚙️ Deterministic Execution Sandbox"] DAG --> T1["Pillar 1: Debt Service (YoY CAF)"] DAG --> T2["Pillar 2: Historical Deleveraging (YoY Debt)"] DAG --> T3["Pillar 3: Cash Flow Coverage (Debt / CAF)"] DAG --> T4["Pillar 4: Balance Sheet Gearing (Debt / Equity)"] DAG --> T5["Pillar 5: Operating Margin Cushion"] T1 & T2 & T3 & T4 & T5 --> PyDec["🐍 Python Decimal Runtime (IEEE-754)
+ Physical Same-Row Grounding [p.X]"] end PyDec --> DraftSynth["📝 Executive Synthesizer
(Draft Decision Memo)"] subgraph AdversarialGate ["🛡️ Adversarial GenRM Gatekeeper"] DraftSynth --> GenRM{"⚖️ GenRM Critic
Adversarial Reward Auditor"} GenRM -->|"❌ REJECT (Polarity contradiction / Tol > 0.05%)"| SelfCorrect["Self-Correction Loop"] SelfCorrect -.-> DraftSynth GenRM -->|"✅ CERTIFIED (100% Grounded & Directionally Verified)"| FinalReport["🏆 Certified ComEx Due Diligence Memo
(Ready for Boardroom Delivery)"] end The Specialist as a Domain Expert, Not a Monolith The Specialist Advisor does not write paragraphs of text. Its sole responsibility is to evaluate available physical table rubrics against declarative banking covenants: @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class LboCovenantPolicyVO : """Invariants of LBO banking feasibility (Domain-Driven Design).""" max_repayment_years : float = 3.5 # Standard senior debt covenant (< 3.5x) critical_repayment_years : float = 5.0 # Junk debt alert threshold max_gearing_pct : float = 100.0 # Max Debt / Equity ratio min_operating_margin_pct : float = 3.0 # Operating safety buffer def evaluate_deal_feasibility ( self , repayment_years : float , gearing_pct : float , margin_pct : float ) -> tuple [ str , str ] : if repayment_years > self . critical_repayment_years or gearing_pct > self . max_gearing_pct : return "UNFAVORABLE" , "Debt repayment horizon exceeds banking covenants." if repayment_years > self . max_repayment_years : return "RESERVED" , "Requires mezzanine financing or subordinated vendor loan." return "FAVORABLE" , "Robust cash flow profile meets senior debt underwriting criteria." Turning Open Questions into an Execution DAG When the Generalist Crew Manager receives the LBO query, it feeds the extracted table headers to the Specialist, which compiles an ExecutionPlanDTO composed of 5 non-negotiable credit pillars: Pillar 1 - Debt Servicing Capacity: Evolution of Self-Financing Capacity ( CAPACITE D'AUTOFINANCEMENT , a proxy for pre-CapEx operating cash flow). Tool: compute_pct_change . Pillar 2 - Historical Deleveraging: Prior trajectory of financial debt ( DETTES FINANCIERES Note E.4 ). Tool: compute_pct_change . Pillar 3 - Debt Coverage (Repayment Horizon / Capacité de Remboursement): Total Financial Debt / CAF (Years of pre-CapEx cash flow required to extinguish debt — a core French banking covenant). Tool: compute_ratio(scale="RAW") . Pillar 4 - Balance Sheet Leverage (Gearing): Financial Debt / Equity ( CAPITAUX PROPRES Note E.1 ). Tool: compute_ratio(scale="PERCENT") . Pillar 5 - Operating Margin Cushion: Operating Income ( RESULTAT D'EXPLOITATION ) / Revenue ( CHIFFRE D'AFFAIRES Note C.1 ). Tool: compute_ratio(scale="PERCENT") . Because each task has designated keywords and an explicit formula, the tasks execute sequentially or in parallel against our Physical Grounding Engine . 3. Grounded Arithmetic: No Hallucinated Numbers As established in Part 1 , all tool calls are executed in Python using exact Decimal arithmetic. As research has repeatedly demonstrated, this triggers sycophancy and confirmation bias : the model rationalizes its mistakes rather than catching them. What does GenRM stand for? GenRM stands for Generative Reward Model —an adversarial verifier pattern introduced in Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction (arXiv:2408.15240) . title: Sending email from FastAPI: SMTP, Resend, templates and testing
author: patrykkomow12
summary:
Every SaaS sends the same handful of emails: confirm your address, reset your password, your payment failed. Here is a small module that sends them over SMTP or an HTTP API, in HTML and plain text, in the user's language, without blocking the event loop, and without an email outage taking your sign-up form down with it. One function, and it never raises The rest of the app calls one function, with the name of an email and its parameters: await send_template ( user . email , "verify" , user . locale , link = link , hours = 48 ) Underneath, a small dataclass and a dispatcher: # app/email/__init__.py @dataclass class Email : to : str subject : str text : str html : str | None = None # Filled by the "memory" backend. Tests read and clear it. outbox : list [ Email ] = [ ] async def send_email ( to : str , subject : str , text : str , html : str | None = None ) -> bool : """Sends one email. Returns False instead of raising when delivery fails, so a mail outage doesn't break sign-ups or payments; the failure is logged.""" email = Email ( to = to , subject = subject , text = text , html = html ) backend = get_settings ( ) . email_backend try : if backend == "memory" : outbox . append ( email ) elif backend == "console" : await backends . send_console ( email ) elif backend == "resend" : await backends . send_resend ( email ) else : await backends . send_smtp ( email ) except Exception : logger . exception ( "Could not send %r to %s" , subject , to ) return False return True Returning False instead of raising is the important decision here. Suppose your SMTP provider has a bad hour. If sending raises, every sign-up during that hour gets a 500 after the account was already created, and a Stripe webhook that tries to send "your payment failed" fails too and gets retried for days. If sending logs and carries on, the user is signed up and can press "send the link again" later. The broad except Exception is deliberate: at this boundary, any failure to deliver means the same thing. One honest limitation: this sends during the request. With a working provider that adds a fraction of a second to a sign-up, and the 15-second timeout below is the worst case. If your app sends a lot of email, or you want retries, move this behind a job queue. For a handful of transactional messages, a queue is more infrastructure than the problem needs. Backends you pick in one setting # app/config.py # "smtp" sends through SMTP_*, "resend" through the Resend API, "console" # prints emails to the log, "memory" keeps them in a list (used by the tests). email_backend : Literal [ "smtp" , "resend" , "console" , "memory" ] = "console" email_from : str = "MySaaS " # Where replies go, if not to EMAIL_FROM (e.g. your support inbox). email_reply_to : str = "" resend_api_key : str = "" smtp_host : str = "localhost" smtp_port : int = 587 smtp_username : str = "" smtp_password : str = "" # "starttls" for port 587, "ssl" for port 465, "none" for a local catcher like Mailpit. smtp_security : Literal [ "starttls" , "ssl" , "none" ] = "starttls" Literal means a typo in EMAIL_BACKEND stops the app at startup, rather than silently sending nothing. console as the default means a fresh checkout works before anyone has configured anything. SMTP without blocking the event loop smtplib is synchronous, and calling it directly in an async route freezes every other request until the mail server answers. You don't need an async SMTP library for this. Run the standard one in a worker thread: # app/email/backends.py def build_message ( email ) -> EmailMessage : """A multipart email: plain text first, HTML as the preferred alternative.""" settings = get_settings ( ) message = EmailMessage ( ) message [ "From" ] = settings . email_from message [ "To" ] = email . to message [ "Subject" ] = email . subject if settings . email_reply_to : message [ "Reply-To" ] = settings . email_reply_to message . set_content ( email . text ) if email . html : message . add_alternative ( email . html , subtype = "html" ) return message def _send_smtp_blocking ( email ) -> None : settings = get_settings ( ) context = ssl . create_default_context ( ) if settings . smtp_security == "ssl" : smtp = smtplib . SMTP_SSL ( settings . smtp_host , settings . smtp_port , context = context , timeout = 15 ) else : smtp = smtplib . SMTP ( settings . smtp_host , settings . smtp_port , timeout = 15 ) with smtp : if settings . smtp_security == "starttls" : smtp . starttls ( context = context ) if settings . smtp_username : smtp . login ( settings . smtp_username , settings . smtp_password ) smtp . send_message ( build_message ( email ) ) async def send_smtp ( email ) -> None : # smtplib blocks, so it runs in a worker thread to keep the event loop free. await asyncio . to_thread ( _send_smtp_blocking , email ) A few details that matter: Set a timeout. smtplib 's default is to wait forever, and a hung connection would hold a worker thread and a user's request with it. Order the parts text first, HTML second. In multipart/alternative , clients show the last part they understand, so HTML wins where it can and text is the fallback. set_content then add_alternative does this for you. EmailMessage , not string formatting. It handles encoding, so Polish characters in a subject work, and it rejects line breaks in headers, which closes off header injection through an address. Some hosts block outgoing mail ports on new servers (Hetzner blocks 25 and 465), so use port 587 with STARTTLS, or an HTTP API. An HTTP API instead of SMTP Providers with an HTTP API work over port 443, which is never blocked, and httpx is already async. This one is for Resend; others look nearly the same: async def send_resend ( email ) -> None : """Resend (resend.com): an HTTP API instead of SMTP. Set RESEND_API_KEY.""" settings = get_settings ( ) payload = { "from" : settings . email_from , "to" : [ email . to ] , "subject" : email . subject , "text" : email . text , } if email . html : payload [ "html" ] = email . html if settings . email_reply_to : payload [ "reply_to" ] = settings . email_reply_to async with httpx . AsyncClient ( timeout = 15 ) as client : response = await client . post ( RESEND_URL , json = payload , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer {settings.resend_api_key}" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) raise_for_status() turns a rejected key or a bounced request into an exception, which send_email catches and logs. Without it, a 401 from the provider would look like a success, and you'd find out from users who never got their email. Templates: words in translation files, one shared layout Writing a separate HTML file for each email means ten copies of the same layout, times the number of languages. Transactional emails all have the same shape anyway: a heading, a few paragraphs, maybe a button, maybe small print. So each email is just its words, stored with the rest of the UI texts: "email.verify.subject": "Confirm your email for {app_name}", "email.verify.heading": "Confirm your email address", "email.verify.body": "First paragraph. Second paragraph.", "email.verify.button": "Confirm email", "email.verify.note": "Small print under the button (optional)." One function turns those keys into a subject and both bodies: # app/email/render.py _env = Environment ( loader = FileSystemLoader ( Path ( __file__ ) . parent . parent / "templates" / "emails" ) , autoescape = select_autoescape ( [ "html" ] ) , trim_blocks = True , lstrip_blocks = True , ) def render_email ( name : str , locale : str , ** params : object ) -> tuple [ str , str , str ] : """Returns (subject, text, html).""" settings = get_settings ( ) params = { "app_name" : settings . app_name , ** params } def text ( part : str ) -> str : return translate ( locale , f "email.{name}.{part}" , ** params ) def optional ( part : str ) -> str | None : key = f "email.{name}.{part}" return translate ( locale , key , ** params ) if has_translation ( locale , key ) else None link = params . get ( "link" ) context = { "lang" : locale , "app_name" : settings . app_name , "subject" : text ( "subject" ) , "heading" : text ( "heading" ) , "paragraphs" : text ( "body" ) . split ( " " ) , "link" : link , "button" : text ( "button" ) if link else None , "note" : optional ( "note" ) , } html = _env . get_template ( "layout.html" ) . render ( context ) plain = _env . get_template ( "layout.txt" ) . render ( context ) return context [ "subject" ] , plain , html The email environment is separate from the one that renders pages, because it has no request and needs no CSRF helpers. select_autoescape(["html"]) escapes values in layout.html and leaves layout.txt alone, so an email address containing @a.b" ) assert "@a.b" in text # plain text needs no escaping def test_smtp_message_is_multipart_with_reply_to ( monkeypatch ) : monkeypatch . setattr ( get_settings ( ) , "email_reply_to" , "support@example.com" ) message = backends . build_message ( email . Email ( to = "ada@example.com" , subject = "Hi" , text = "Plain" , html = "

Rich

" ) ) assert message [ "Reply-To" ] == "support@example.com" assert [ part . get_content_type ( ) for part in message . iter_parts ( ) ] == [ "text/plain" , "text/html" , ] And the HTTP backend without touching the network, using httpx.MockTransport : async def test_resend_backend ( monkeypatch ) : requests = [ ] def handler ( request : httpx . Request ) -> httpx . Response : requests . append ( request ) return httpx . Response ( 200 , json = { "id" : "email_123" } ) real_client = httpx . AsyncClient monkeypatch . setattr ( backends . httpx , "AsyncClient" , lambda ** kw : real_client ( transport = httpx . MockTransport ( handler ) ) , ) settings = get_settings ( ) monkeypatch . setattr ( settings , "email_backend" , "resend" ) monkeypatch . setattr ( settings , "resend_api_key" , "re_test_key" ) assert await send_email ( "ada@example.com" , "Hi" , "Plain" , "

Rich

" ) assert requests [ 0 ] . headers [ "authorization" ] == "Bearer re_test_key" Getting delivered The code is the easy half. The first thing that goes wrong in production is usually mail landing in spam, and no code fixes that: Send from your own domain , through a provider, not directly from your server's IP address. Add SPF and DKIM records to your DNS. Your provider gives you the exact values. Add a DMARC record too; large mailbox providers now expect it from anyone sending at volume. Keep transactional mail separate from marketing , ideally on a different subdomain, so a newsletter complaint doesn't hurt your password resets. Send yourself the real thing after you deploy: sign up with a Gmail and an Outlook address and read the results. Checklist One send_template() that logs failures and returns False instead of raising. The backend chosen by one validated setting, with memory for tests. smtplib in asyncio.to_thread , always with a timeout. raise_for_status() on API backends. Words in translation files; one HTML and one text layout; autoescape on HTML only. The user's language stored on the account; links built from BASE_URL . Mailpit in development; a test that renders every email in every language. SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up before launch. This email module is part of getpylaunch , a FastAPI SaaS starter I sell, with its account and billing emails already written in English and Polish.

title: How We Update Client Websites Without Breaking the Live Site
author: aimEncoders
summary: Website updates break sites in boring, predictable ways: a plugin conflicts with the theme, a deploy overwrites a config, a form silently stops submitting. The fix is not better luck. It is a repeatable process: staging, backup, deploy, verify, rollback plan. Here is the exact process we run at aimEncoders on every client update, and the checks we run after each deploy. Why a Small Update Can Cause a Big Problem Most updates are routine. A plugin releases a new version, WordPress pushes a security fix, a theme gets a compatibility patch. The button says "update now", and it looks like a one-click job. The risk is what sits behind that button. Your site is made of pieces built by different people at different times: the core platform, the theme, a handful of plugins, custom code, and third-party tools for payments, bookings, or chat. An update to one piece can disagree with another. The site still loads, the homepage still looks right, and the problem hides on a page nobody checked. A customer finds it first. That is why we never treat an update as a simple click. The work that keeps a site safe happens before and after the update itself, not during it. How We Update a Client Website, Step by Step 1. Test the change on a staging copy first A staging site is a private copy of the live website. It looks and behaves the same way, but visitors never see it. We apply the update there first, so any problem appears in a safe place instead of in front of customers. Say a client wants a new version of their booking plugin. On staging, we install it and walk through the whole booking flow: pick a date, choose a time, submit the form, check the confirmation. If the date picker breaks or a step goes blank, we find out here and fix it here, and the live site never feels a thing. Only when staging behaves do we move forward. We run the same kind of checks on staging that we run before a launch, including our Playwright checks on the key pages and forms. 2. Take a full backup before touching anything Before we change the live site, we take a complete backup: the files, the database, the images, and the settings. WordPress itself recommends backing up before updates, and we follow that advice on every site we manage, not just the big ones. You can read the official guidance in the WordPress updating documentation ( https://wordpress.org/documentation/article/updating-wordpress/ ). A backup only helps if it is fresh and complete. A copy from three months ago will not bring back last week's enquiries or yesterday's orders. So we take the backup right before the update, and we store it away from the live site, so a problem with the hosting account does not take the backup down with it. This step takes minutes. Recovering a site without a backup can take days. 3. Deploy the change, then check the parts that earn money Once staging passes and the backup is in place, we apply the update to the live site. Then the real work starts: checking that the site still does its job. We do not just load the homepage and call it done. The homepage can look perfect while the contact form quietly fails. We open the pages visitors use most, submit a test enquiry through the form, and check that it arrives. On a store, we walk through the cart and checkout. On a booking site, we test a booking end to end. We check the menus, the buttons, and the pages on a real phone, because that is how most Pakistani customers will see the site. This is the step that catches the problems nobody expects. A plugin update once changed how a form handled phone numbers, and the form looked fine until someone actually tried to submit it. The homepage check would have missed it. The form check caught it in minutes. 4. Keep a rollback plan ready Even with staging and backups, a live server can surprise you. A plugin can behave differently on the live server than it did on staging. A third-party service can stop responding at exactly the wrong moment. So before every significant update, we decide in advance how we would undo it. Sometimes rolling back means reversing one plugin to its previous version. Sometimes it means restoring files from the backup we just took. Either way, the decision is made before the update, not in a panic after something breaks. We also think about what changed since the backup: restoring an old database on a busy store could wipe out new orders, so the recovery has to be planned around the site's real activity, not just its files. 5. Pick a quiet hour Timing matters. Updating a store in the middle of its busiest afternoon is asking for trouble, even with everything else done right. So we look at when the site is actually quiet and schedule bigger updates for then. For most Pakistani businesses, that means late at night or early in the morning, when traffic is low and few customers are browsing. The right hour is different for every site, so we check the site's own analytics instead of guessing. A site serving customers overseas may have its quiet hours at a completely different time of day. Small security patches do not always need a maintenance window, but anything that touches the theme, the checkout, or a booking flow gets a quiet slot and enough time to test properly. 6. Tell the client what changed Most business owners do not want a technical report. They want to know three things: what changed, whether anything will look different, and whether the site is ready for customers again. So that is what we tell them, in plain words, before and after the work. Before a bigger update, we explain what is being updated and why, and whether visitors will notice anything. If a design change is involved, we share a preview from staging so the client can approve it before it goes live. After the update, we confirm what was done and what we checked. If something took longer than expected, we say so, and we say why. A client who knows what is happening trusts the process. The Final Check Before We Call It Done Every update ends with the same short list, and we do not call the work finished until it passes. We open the homepage and the most important service and product pages. We submit the contact form and confirm the message arrives. We click through the menus and check the links. We look at the site on a phone and a tablet. We check images, buttons, and anything interactive. On a store, we test the cart and checkout with a test payment, never a real order. We watch for error messages and slow pages. The list is short on purpose. It covers the things a customer would hit first, and it takes minutes. When an Update Still Goes Wrong Sometimes it still goes wrong. A plugin update can reveal a conflict that staging did not show, or a third-party tool can change something on its side overnight. Pretending that never happens would be dishonest. What matters is the response. First, we stop and find out what broke. We do not pile more changes on top of a problem we do not understand yet. Then we judge the impact: a spacing issue on a secondary page is one thing, a checkout that will not take payments is another. If the problem is serious, we roll back to the version that worked, using the backup and the plan we made before the update. Only once the site is stable do we investigate the cause, test a fix on staging, and try again. The client hears about it the same day, in plain language: what broke, what we did about it, and what happens next. Why This Process Matters for Your Business A careful update process buys you four things. It keeps customers moving: a form that works and a checkout that completes mean enquiries and orders keep coming in while the site improves in the background. It protects your content and your data: backups and staging mean years of pages, posts, and customer records are never one bad click away from disappearing. It protects your search visibility: a broken page or a sudden error can push a site down in Google. And it gives you confidence: when you know updates are handled carefully, you stop worrying about the website and get back to running the business. Your website will need updates for as long as it exists. Security patches, new features, better design, faster pages. The question is never whether to update. It is whether the updates happen carefully or carelessly. We choose carefully, every time. If your website needs regular maintenance, talk to us. aimEncoders ( https://aimencoders.com ) handles updates, backups, and testing for businesses across Pakistan, and our web development services ( https://aimencoders.com/services ) start with the same careful approach on every project. We also wrote a guide to getting more enquiries from your website ( https://aimencoders.com/blog/how-to-get-more-enquiries-without-more-traffic ), which pairs well with keeping the site itself healthy. Frequently Asked Questions Can updating a website break it? Yes. An update can clash with a plugin, a theme, or a third-party tool, and the problem may only show on one page or one device. Testing on staging, taking a backup, and checking the site after the update are how you keep that risk small. Should website updates be tested before they go live? For anything beyond a tiny patch, yes. A staging copy lets you test the update without touching the live site. If something breaks, you fix it in private and your customers never see the problem. What is a staging website? It is a private copy of your live site used for testing. It looks and works the same way, but only your team can see it. Changes are tried there first, then moved to the live site once they pass. Do I need a backup before updating my website? Yes, always take a fresh one before a significant update. It should cover the files and the database, and it should be stored away from the live site. If an update goes badly, that backup is your way back. Can website updates be done without downtime? Most can. Small updates usually finish with no interruption at all. Bigger changes may need a short maintenance window, which is why we schedule them during quiet hours and keep the work as quick as possible. How often should a business website be updated? Ongoing, not once a year. Security patches should go out promptly, plugins and themes should be reviewed regularly, and backups and checks should run on a schedule. A site with daily orders or bookings needs more frequent attention than a simple brochure site. title: I built a PDF toolkit that never uploads your files
author: Jose Dario
summary: Every "free" PDF converter I tried asked me to upload the file first. For a bank statement or a signed contract, that is the whole problem: you are handing a document to a server you know nothing about, and hoping it gets deleted. So I built ConvUp , a converter that runs entirely in the browser. No upload endpoint, no account, no watermark. What is actually possible in a browser today More than I expected. The stack: pdf-lib — create, merge, split, rotate, number pages, draw text, embed images. pdf.js — render pages to canvas for JPG export and for OCR input. Tesseract.js — OCR in a Web Worker, with the language model cached after first use. JSZip — build .docx and .zip files client-side. Web Audio + a Worker — decode and re-encode audio to MP3/WAV. The only network requests are the app's own static files and, for OCR, the Tesseract language model from a public CDN. Your document never appears in any request. That is verifiable: open DevTools, go to Network, convert a file. Rotating a PDF is one attribute, not a re-render The first tool I wrote was "rotate pages". It is four lines: const doc = await PDFDocument . load ( bytes ) ; const page = doc . getPages ( ) [ i ] ; const current = page . getRotation ( ) . angle || 0 ; page . setRotation ( degrees ( ( current + 90 ) % 360 ) ) ; No pixels are touched. A PDF page carries a rotation attribute that the viewer applies when drawing; changing it fixes a sideways scan without recompressing anything, so text stays selectable and images keep their resolution. That distinction matters: most online tools re-render the page to an image and hand you back a heavier, blurrier file. The three parts that are genuinely hard 1. Scanned PDFs. A scan has no text layer. Converting it to Word gives you an empty document. The honest fix is OCR first, then convert — and even then, accuracy depends on 300 dpi, straight pages and printed text. Handwriting and shadows still fail. 2. Multi-column layouts. A PDF does not store paragraphs; it stores text fragments at coordinates. To rebuild a document you group fragments by baseline and guess the reading order. Single column: fine. Two or three columns, tables, footers mixed into the body: the order comes out scrambled and needs manual fixes. I decided not to pretend otherwise and said so in the UI. 3. Memory. Everything happens in the tab. A 200 MB audio file or a 600-page scan can kill it. The limits (15 minutes of audio, 40 PDFs to merge, 500 MB per file) exist because the browser is the machine doing the work. The trade-off nobody mentions Local processing means the user's device pays the cost. A 40-page scanned PDF compressed in the browser takes seconds to minutes depending on the CPU, while a server farm would do it in one. I think it is the right trade for documents you would not email to a stranger, but it is a trade. Ads, stated plainly The site is free and has ads. They load when you open a tool, and in the EU, the UK and Switzerland only after you accept. No pop-ups on the homepage, no forced clicks, no "wait 30 seconds to download". The file is generated before any ad gate. What I would do differently I would start with the guides, not the tools. Search traffic came from "compress a PDF for a 2 MB form", not from "pdf converter". I would test on a low-end Android phone from day one. That is where memory limits actually bite. I would not build eleven tools before validating one. If you want to try it: convup.lodcrafttools.workers.dev . If something breaks, tell me which file and what you expected — I would rather fix a real failure than add a feature nobody asked for.

title: How to Learn Claude AI in One Day: A Practical Guide for Developers
author: DevSpire Hub
summary: AI coding assistants are becoming part of everyday software development. But let's be honest: how many times have you asked an AI to generate code, only to receive generic explanations, incomplete implementations, or code that doesn't even match your project requirements? The problem isn't always the AI model. Often, it's how we communicate with it. Claude AI can be much more than a chatbot. When you understand its capabilities and learn how to provide clear instructions, relevant context, and structured requirements, you can turn it into a valuable development partner. Whether you're a beginner, Python developer, full-stack engineer, or AI enthusiast, learning how to use Claude effectively can improve your research, coding, documentation, and productivity. I've created a visual cheat sheet covering 12 important Claude features to help you understand what Claude offers and where each capability fits into a practical workflow. The Claude AI Cheat Sheet The poster covers these 12 features: Claude Chat – Ask questions, write content, analyze information, and solve problems. Extended Thinking – Explore more complex problems with deeper reasoning. Claude API – Integrate Claude into applications and automated workflows. Memory – Retain useful preferences and context where supported. Artifacts – Create interactive content, documents, code, and other working outputs. Cowork – Work with files and documents through supported desktop workflows. Claude in Chrome – Use browser-based assistance for web research and tasks. Claude Code – Work with codebases, terminal workflows, and software development tasks. Connectors – Connect Claude with supported external tools and services. Plugins – Extend capabilities through available integrations and tools. Skills – Use reusable instructions for specialized workflows. Projects – Organize files, instructions, and conversations around ongoing work. 5 Practical Techniques to Get Better Results from Claude Knowing the features is only the starting point. The real value comes from learning how to use them effectively. Here are five techniques worth practicing. Write Clear, Specific Prompts A vague prompt usually produces a vague answer. Instead of asking Claude to build something without explaining the requirements, describe the task, expected behavior, technology stack, and constraints. Bad Prompt: Build a login page using React. Good Prompt: Build a responsive login page using React and Tailwind CSS. Requirements: Email and password fields Client-side form validation Password visibility toggle Loading state during submission Accessible labels and error messages Keep the components reusable. Use functional components and React hooks. Return the complete implementation with a short explanation of the component structure. Why it works: Claude receives a clear definition of the expected output instead of having to guess your requirements. Use System Instructions and Negative Constraints System instructions establish the behavior and boundaries you expect from an AI assistant. Negative constraints specify what it should avoid. For example, when working on an existing application, you may want Claude to preserve the architecture instead of rewriting everything. Bad Prompt: Improve my backend code. Good Prompt: Act as a senior Python backend developer. Review the provided FastAPI code. Instructions: Preserve the existing architecture. Follow PEP 8 conventions. Use type hints. Identify security and validation issues. Explain important changes. Constraints: Do not introduce unnecessary dependencies. Do not remove existing API endpoints. Do not change response schemas without explaining why. Return the improved code and a summary. Why it works: Clear behavioral instructions and constraints help keep the response aligned with your project's requirements. Use Few-Shot Prompting Few-shot prompting means providing examples of the output you expect. This is especially useful when you need consistent formatting, naming conventions, documentation, or structured responses. Bad Prompt: Generate API documentation for my endpoints. Good Prompt: Generate API documentation using this format. Example: Endpoint: GET /api/users Purpose: Retrieve all users. Parameters: page, limit Response: JSON array of user objects. Now document these endpoints: GET /api/products POST /api/products DELETE /api/products/{id} Follow the same structure and level of detail. Do not invent request or response fields. Use the supplied source code as reference. Why it works: Examples demonstrate the expected structure more precisely than general instructions. Request Structured Output with Markdown or JSON When working with technical information, structured output is easier to read, reuse, validate, and process programmatically. You can request Markdown tables, JSON objects, checklists, or code blocks depending on your workflow. Bad Prompt: Explain the API response. Good Prompt: Analyze the following API response. Return valid JSON using this structure: { "status": "", "success": true, "data": [], "errors": [], "summary": "" } Requirements: Use the supplied response only. Preserve the original field names. Do not invent missing values. Return JSON without Markdown fences. Why it works: A defined output format makes the result easier to integrate into scripts, applications, and documentation. Iterate, Verify, and Improve AI Output Never assume AI-generated code is correct just because it looks convincing. Treat Claude as an assistant, not an unquestionable source of truth. Use follow-up prompts to review, test, and improve its output. For coding tasks, Claude Code can also help inspect project files and work through development workflows. Bad Prompt: Is this code correct? Good Prompt: Review the following Python function. Check for: Logical errors Edge cases Invalid input handling Security concerns Performance issues Then: Suggest improvements. Write relevant pytest test cases. Explain potential failure scenarios. Do not claim tests have passed unless they have actually been executed. Here is the code: [PASTE YOUR CODE] Why it works: Verification encourages critical thinking and helps catch problems before they reach production. How to Practice These Claude Features in One Day You don't need to master every feature immediately. Start with a focused learning schedule. Time| Learning activity 9:00–10:00 AM| Explore Claude Chat and prompt fundamentals 10:00–11:00 AM| Practice structured prompts and extended thinking 11:00 AM–12:00 PM| Experiment with Artifacts 12:00–1:00 PM| Explore Projects and persistent context 2:00–3:00 PM| Learn Claude Code fundamentals 3:00–4:00 PM| Explore connectors, skills, and integrations 4:00–5:00 PM| Build a small practical project 5:00–6:00 PM| Review, test, and improve your results This is a suggested introduction schedule, not a promise of mastery in one day. A Small Project to Put Your Knowledge into Practice Try building a simple AI-powered document assistant. Your project could include: A document upload interface. An AI-powered question-and-answer feature. Document summarization. Structured responses. A simple backend API. Basic input validation and error handling. Use Claude to help plan the architecture, generate starter code, explain implementation decisions, and review your work. Most importantly, understand the code you build. Don't simply copy and paste AI-generated solutions. Final Thoughts Learning Claude isn't about memorizing every feature or discovering one perfect prompt. It's about understanding how to communicate requirements, provide context, choose the right tools, and validate the results. Start with Claude Chat, experiment with Projects and Artifacts, explore Claude Code, and gradually introduce AI into your everyday development workflow. Learn the tools. Build real projects. Verify everything. Keep improving. Let's Connect! If you found this guide useful: Bookmark this article for future reference. title: I stopped letting Opus write my code (and my weekly quota survived)
author: Yiğit Güldal
summary: one day claude ate 62% of my weekly quota in a single day. i was letting opus write every line. so i changed one rule: claude plans and reviews, cheaper models write the code. the split lead (claude): reads the task, splits it into small pieces with the exact files and an acceptance check, then reviews the diff workers (codex, opencode, free models): write the code for one piece each lead again: runs the tests itself, reads the real diff, sends it back if its off the trick is the spec. a worker that gets "fix the login bug" burns tokens wandering around the repo. a worker that gets "edit src/auth.ts lines 40-80, expected behaviour X, run npm test auth , short report" finishes fast and cheap. what broke when i did it by hand 5 terminals, copy pasting context between them forgetting which agent was on which file two agents editing the same file a long build dying at the 5 hour limit in the middle of a task what fixed it one git worktree per agent, so they never share a checkout one memory file in the repo, so the next session doesnt start from zero the lead always looks at the real diff, never trusts the worker's report you can do all of this with plain terminals and a CLAUDE.md. i ended up building a desktop app for it, foxpit , but the split works without it too.

title: ChatGPT for financial advisors: the plan decides the compliance answer
author: PJ (Prakshal Jain)
summary: Disclosure: I co-founded Mitosis Labs, which runs Private SuperIntelligence. This is an adaptation of the original guide written for registered investment advisers. General information, not legal advice. ChatGPT is safe for financial advisors only on a business plan your firm has approved, set up and put under its compliance program. Under the hood, that is a data-flow question with three parts: does the plan train on the input, where does the record go, and who else now holds customer information. Training and retention by plan Free, Plus, Pro: trains by default unless you turn off "Improve the model for everyone". Deleted chats are removed within 30 days, with security and legal exceptions. Temporary Chat: no training, but a copy may be kept up to 30 days. Business and Enterprise: no training by default; workspace admins set retention. API: no training by default; abuse logs up to 30 days by default, Zero Data Retention for approved customers. Edge cases: a thumbs up or down can send the whole conversation for training, even after you opt out. And in the New York Times copyright case, a federal court ordered OpenAI in May 2025 to preserve ChatGPT output logs that would otherwise have been deleted, an obligation that ended on September 26, 2025. The record and the vendor SEC Rule 204-2(a)(7) covers copies of written communications sent relating to any recommendation made or advice given. It says nothing about who, or what, drafted the message, so an AI-drafted client email is still an email you sent. Required records are kept for at least five years. Amended Regulation S-P defines a service provider as any person or entity that receives, maintains, processes or otherwise is permitted access to customer information through its services to the firm. Pipe client data into a model and the vendor joins your oversight program, including notice within 72 hours of a breach affecting a customer information system it maintains. For builders, the records row matters most: OpenAI's Compliance Platform for Enterprise and Edu feeds eDiscovery, DLP and SIEM tools; Copilot interactions are searchable with retention set in Microsoft Purview; for Claude for Work, ask Anthropic which archiving routes your plan supports. Private SuperIntelligence from Mitosis Labs works across a firm's own email, documents and data, answers with citations, and acts only within the permissions the firm sets. Each deployment is built for one client, and the provider keeps no copy of the work, trains nothing on it and cannot see the outputs. title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Google's Fast Model for Everyday Coding
author: Mohammad Hassan Amer
summary: Have you ever asked a search engine a question with three parts, a typo, and a very specific detail, all in one go, and watched it answer only the easy part? Google introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, 2026, a fast model built for everyday coding and multi-step work where an AI carries out a task on its own. It is the third member of the Gemini 4 family, next to Carbon and Argon, and it is already rolling out across Search, the Gemini app, Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, and Google Antigravity. The fast one in the family Here is the simplest way I think about it. Carbon and Argon are the deep thinkers, for long, hard reasoning problems, the kind where you want the model to sit with a tricky architecture decision or an unclear bug for a while. Hydrogen is the one that gets on with the job. It is built for rapid execution: writing code, running tests, and checking changes without making you wait. Google positions it as the model for the work you do all day, every day, rather than the rare problem that needs a whole afternoon of thinking. That split feels familiar to me. Building software has always had both jobs. Somebody has to draw the plan, and somebody has to lay the bricks quickly and neatly. A team with only planners never ships anything, and a team with only fast hands and no plan builds the wrong thing, quickly. Photo by Gabriel Heinzer on Unsplash Working as a pair That pairing is not just a marketing idea. In Antigravity, Google's coding platform, a new feature called Orchestrator switches between Carbon and Hydrogen inside the same session, so Carbon can coordinate while Hydrogen powers the worker agents that build and test changes at the same time. On its own, Hydrogen is also a step up from the model it replaces, Gemini 3.8 Flash: Google says it finishes tasks 2.5 times faster at its default setting, with its Terminal-Bench 4.1 score rising from 18.2 percent to 57 percent. Those are Google's own numbers, so take them as a claim to watch rather than a settled fact. What it costs, and where you will meet it For developers, the pricing is simple: $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, flat across its one million token context window. It comes with four thinking levels, low, medium, high, and a new extra high level called xhigh, so you can pick how much reasoning a task is worth before you pay for it in time and tokens. But most people will meet Hydrogen without ever opening an API dashboard. In Google Search it is now the default model in AI Mode, and it handles the hardest questions in AI Overviews. Google says it breaks a complicated question into its parts and answers each one, even when the question has typos or very specific details. The Verge reported the same rollout on November 12, 2026, quoting Robby Stein, Google's VP of product for Search, who called it the biggest model upgrade to Search yet. Fast is a feature, not a shortcut Speed on its own is not very interesting. What matters is whether a fast model stays careful while it hurries. Google says Hydrogen is more disciplined when a tool call fails or a search comes back empty, and that it adapts instead of guessing its way forward. If that holds up, it matters more than any benchmark, because the whole point of an everyday model is that you trust it with the boring, repeated work. So here is my question for you. If the fast model gets good enough to handle the routine coding, the searching, and the first draft of a task, what do you want to spend your own thinking time on? The planning, the judgment calls, the parts no model can do for you? That is the work Hydrogen is supposed to free up. Cover photo by Mohammad Rahmani on Unsplash

title: Five coding agents, five formats, one table
author: Dmitriy Solodukha
summary: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and DeepSeek Harness each record their work differently, and three of the differences give a believable wrong number. This post compares how five coding agents — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and DeepSeek Harness — write down what they did: where the record lives, its format, how it counts cached tokens, whether it states a cost, and where it names the model. Then it shows the one table Caprock turns all five into, so their numbers can be added up. Update, 2026-10-20: Caprock now reads a sixth, Hermes Agent, from its own SQLite database, and carries Hermes's cost figure through as it does OpenCode's. A reader looked at Caprock and guessed what it does underneath: "parsing JSON, and sweating to build a coherent image out of huge and heavy JSON files." He was right, and it is the part of the product nobody sees. None of the five writes its record the same way, none promises to keep its format as it is, and Claude Code deletes its record after 30 days . How each agent records its work How each agent records its work, read on one machine, 1 October 2026Agent Where it lives Format Cached tokens Reports its cost Model named in Claude Code ~/.claude/projects JSON lines beside fresh input no each reply Codex ~/.codex/sessions JSON lines inside input no base instructions, 96 of 100 OpenCode its SQLite database SQL rows own column yes each session Gemini CLI a telemetry file, if asked OTel log reads, no writes no each response DeepSeek Harness session.v3.jsonl.zstd JSON lines, zstd beside fresh input no each reply "Cached tokens" is how the cached part of a prompt is counted; OTel is OpenTelemetry. Codex also writes token counts as running totals. Caprock reads Gemini CLI from a telemetry file it asks for when it starts a session. (As of 2026-10-20: Gemini CLI does keep its own session history, under ~/.gemini/tmp//chats/; Caprock does not read it.) Three ways to get a believable wrong answer Reading the files is not the hard part. The obvious reading of each can give you a number that looks right and is not. Cached tokens counted twice. Claude Code reports fresh input and cache reads side by side. Codex reports the whole prompt as input, with the cached part as a subset of it. Treat the two the same way and every cached Codex token is billed twice — once at full price. Tokens counted twice. Codex writes both a running total and a per-turn figure, and often writes the same sample twice in a row. Summing the per-turn figure on one real session gave 261,111 tokens; the true count was 137,739. The model in the wrong place. Codex names the model in a turn context in 4 transcripts out of 100. In the other 96 it is inside the session's base instructions. Read only the obvious field and most of your Codex work has no model, so no price. None of these mistakes raises a parsing error. A wrong number can sit on a dashboard looking perfectly ordinary. One table Caprock reads all five as they are written and turns each into the same rows: one per turn, tool call or lifecycle event, with the same columns whichever agent produced it — agent, model, fresh input, cache read, cache write, output, cost, the folder the work touched. That table is yours to take out. On my machine, on 1 October: $ caprock export > record.tsv $ wc -l record.tsv 305162 record.tsv Three hundred thousand rows from four agents, in about five seconds, as TSV, CSV or JSON lines. It reads the database without writing to it, works with Caprock stopped, and leaves out prompts and replies unless you ask for them. Here is one reply from each agent in it: One reply from each agent, from the same export — four replies of different sizes, not a cost comparisonAgent Model tokens_in tokens_out cache_read cost_usd Claude Code claude-opus-5-5 2 1,073 308,787 $0.198 Codex gpt-6-astra 4,656 116 55,552 $0.108 OpenCode deepseek-v4-pro 26,983 1,515 5,120 $0.057 DeepSeek Harness deepseek-v4-pro 128 823 121,472 $0.0012 Columns 3, 8–11 and 14 of the export, cost rounded. Gemini CLI has no row: Caprock records only the Gemini sessions it starts, and the record held none. Look at the tokens_in column. Claude Code's fresh input is 2 tokens, because almost everything came from the cache; Codex's is 4,656 because the cached part has already been taken out of it. In the files they came from, those two numbers mean different things. Here they mean the same thing. Four of the five report tokens and no cost, so Caprock prices them from a dated table of each provider's list prices. OpenCode computes its own cost, and that figure is kept as it is — two arithmetics over the same tokens would give one session two totals. Why this is the part worth having When a vendor changes its format, the table stays the same. The work of noticing is done once here, instead of by everyone trying to count what their agents cost. The columns are documented in the schema . It is plain SQLite on your disk, with network features off by default.
